items.text: **Option 1: Adenomyosis.** Typically presents with a uniformly enlarged, boggy uterus. Histologically shows endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium, not just smooth muscle cells.

**Option 2: Leiomyosarcoma.** Rare malignant smooth muscle tumor. Histologically shows significant atypia, high mitotic rate, and areas of necrosis. Patients may present with rapidly growing mass and systemic symptoms.

**Option 3: Endometrial carcinoma.** Typically presents with abnormal uterine bleeding, especially postmenopausal bleeding. Histology shows malignant endometrial glandular cells, not smooth muscle cells.

blocks.text: **Liposarcoma:** Malignant adipose tissue tumour. Most common adult sarcoma. Typically occur in the sixth and seventh decades. Develop in proximal extremities and retroperitoneum.
**Three subtypes:**

items.text: **Well-differentiated:** chromosome 12 amplification, including p53 inhibitor MDM2.
**Myxoid:** t(12;16) translocation.
Pleomorphic

blocks.text: **Biopsy:**

items.text: **Well-differentiated:** Mature adipocytes with scattered atypical spindle cells.
**Myxoid:** Abundant basophilic extracellular matrix, arborizing capillaries ( chicken wire blood vessels ) and primitive fat cells ( lipoblasts ).
**Pleomorphic:** Sheets of anaplastic cells with bizarre nuclei and immature adipocytes, called lipoblasts.

blocks.text: **OTHER OPTIONS:**

items.text: **Option 1:** Lipoma is the most common benign soft tissue tumor of fat in adults and, upon biopsy, reveals mature fat cells with peripheral nuclei.
**Option 3:** Leiomyosarcomas are malignant, painless, firm masses arising from smooth muscle. These tumours are composed of eosinophilic spindle cells with blunt-ended, cigar shaped nuclei.
**Option 4:** Fibrosarcoma is a malignant tumour of fibroblasts with a \"herringbone\" architecture.

blocks.text: **Aneurysmal Bone Cyst (ABC):** Affects all age groups, with most cases in adolescence. Characterised by multiloculated blood-filled spaces (Option 1).

items.text: **Location:** Femur, tibia, and posterior vertebral body (Option 2).
**Genetics:** Chromosome 17p13 rearrangements result in fusion of the USP6 coding region in 70% cases. (Option 3) Highly expressed osteoblast genes like CDH11. USP6 upregulates NF-κB activity.

**Biopsy:** Blood-filled cystic spaces separated by thin, tan-white septa made up of spindle cells, osteoclast-like giant cells. Approximately one-third cases contain densely calcified, basophilic metaplastic matrix called blue bone (Option 4). Necrosis is uncommon.

blocks.text: A non-ossifying fibroma is the most likely diagnosis. A biopsy finding suggestive of storiform pattern made by benign spindle cells with scattered osteoclast-type giant cells.

**Non-Ossifying Fibroma:** Developmental defect in which fibrous connective tissue replaces bone. Age group: children and adolescents. Arise eccentrically in the metaphysis of the distal femur and proximal tibia.
Masses growing to 5 or 6 cm are classified as non-ossifying fibromas.
**Morphology:**

items.text: **Gross:** Yellow-brown.

**Microscopic:** Bland fibroblasts arranged in a storiform (pinwheel) pattern and macrophages with foamy cytoplasm or multinucleated giant cells with osteoblastic rimming. Hemosiderin is commonly present.

blocks.text: **Fibrous Dysplasia:** It is a benign childhood tumour caused by GNAS1 mutations, characterised by immature normal bone components and disorganised growth plates, linked to McCune- Albright syndrome. The components of normal bone are present, but do not differentiate into mature structure.
**Types:** Can be monostotic or polyostotic.

items.text: **Monostotic:** more common in craniofacial bones and femur.
**Polystotic:** commonly affected are pelvis, femur and tibia.

blocks.text: **McCuneAlbright Syndrome:** Commonly presented as precocious sexual development, mainly in girls. Polyostotic disease associated with café-au-lait skin pigmentations and endocrine abnormalities. Café-au-lait macules: dark large macules with irregular serpiginous borders on the same side of the body as the bone lesions.
**Mazabraud syndrome:** Fibrous dysplasia associated with soft tissue myxomas.
**Morphology:**

items.text: **Gross:** Tan-white, gritty structure.
**Nodules of hyaline cartilage:** disorganized growth plates.
Shepherd's crook deformity
**Microscopy:** Curvilinear trabeculae of woven bone that lack conspicuous osteoblastic rimming in a background of fibrous tissue ( Chinese letter pattern).

blocks.text: Reiter Syndrome (also known as Reactive Arthritis) is associated with HLA-B27.
**It is defined by the triad of:**

items.text: Arthritis
Nongonococcal urethritis or cervicitis
Conjunctivitis

blocks.text: **Etiology:** It occurs days to weeks after genitourinary (Chlamydia) or gastrointestinal (Shigella, Salmonella, Yersinia, Campylobacter, and Clostrdioides difficile) infections. HIV-positive patients may also be affected.
**Clinical features:**

items.text: **Onset:** Acute
Enthesitis, oligoarthritis and/or spinal inflammation.
Lower limb joints and entheses are predominantly affected.
Systemic disturbances like fever and weight loss.
Achilles insertional enthesitis/tendonitis or plantar fasciitis may also be present.
The first attack of arthritis is usually self-limiting, but recurrent or chronic arthritis can develop.
Low back pain and stiffness (due to enthesitis and osteitis)
Sacroiliitis

blocks.text: **Extra-articular features:**

items.text: **Circinate balanitis:** Starts as vesicles on the coronal margin of the prepuce and glans penis, later rupturing to form superficial erosions with minimal surrounding erythema, some coalescing to give a circular pattern.

**Keratoderma blennorrhagica:** Begins as discrete waxy, yellow-brown vesico-papules with desquamating margins, occasionally coalescing to form large crusty plaques on the palms and soles of the feet.
Pustular psoriasis
Nail dystrophy with subungual hyperkeratosis
Mouth ulcers
Conjunctivitis
Uveitis

**HLA-DR3 (Option A)** is associated with autoimmune diseases such as Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), Type 1 diabetes, and Graves' disease, but it is not linked to Reiter's Syndrome (Reactive Arthritis), which is specifically associated with HLA-B27.
**HLA-DQ8 (Option C):** is associated with Celiac disease and some autoimmune disorders, such as Type 1 diabetes, but it is not linked to Reiter's Syndrome.
**HLA-DR4 (Option D):** is associated with autoimmune conditions such as Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) and Type 1 diabetes.

blocks.text: The clinical scenario, along with the image showing small, round, uniform cells and positive immunohistochemistry for synaptophysin and MIC2 (CD99) in the diaphysis of long bones like the tibia, is characteristic of Ewing sarcoma.
**Ewing’s sarcoma:** It is a malignant bone tumour characterized by primitive round cells without obvious differentiation. Approximately 80% of patients are younger than 20 years of age.

items.text: Males are affected slightly more often than Females.
It usually arises in the diaphysis of long tubular bones, especially the femur and in the flat bones of the pelvis, and presents as a painful, enlarging mass.
The most common mutation (>90% of the cases) is t(11;22)(q24;q12).
**Morphology:** The tumour is soft, tan-white, and frequently contains areas of haemorrhage and necrosis.
It comprises sheets of uniform, small, round cells with scant cytoplasm that may be clear due to abundant glycogen.
Homer-Wright rosettes (pseudorosettes) are rounded cell clusters with a central fibrillary core; their presence indicates neuroectodermal differentiation.
**Specific markers:** CD99+ (MIC2) positive.
Fibrous septae may also be present, but there is little stroma.
Geographic necrosis may be prominent.
Chemotherapy-induced necrosis is a positive prognostic indicator.

**Osteosarcoma (Option A):** is a type of bone cancer originating from cells that produce new bone tissue. It often presents with pain and swelling in the affected bone, and X-rays may show a characteristic "sunburst" or "spiculated" appearance. Histologically, osteosarcoma is characterized by the production of osteoid, a bone-like substance formed by the tumour cells.

**Metastatic Neuroblastoma (Option C):** is a cancer that develops from immature nerve cells and most commonly occurs in young children. It can originate in areas like the adrenal glands or nerve tissues in the neck, chest, or abdomen. While it may metastasize to the bone and cause lytic lesions, it is not typically associated with a periosteal reaction or positive immunohistochemistry for synaptophysin and MIC2.

**Osteoclastoma (Option D):** , also known as a giant cell tumour of bone, is a benign tumour that mainly affects young adults. It is characterized by multinucleated giant cells and osteoclast-like cells. X-rays usually show a lytic lesion with a "soap bubble" appearance. However, it is not typically associated with a periosteal reaction or positive immunohistochemical findings for synaptophysin and MIC2.

blocks.text: The clinical presentation and histopathological image reveal numerous multinucleated giant cells within a bone lesion, which highly suggests Osteoclastoma (Giant cell tumour of bone).

**Giant cell tumour (Osteoclastoma):** It is a benign but locally aggressive tumour, characterised by numerous multinucleated osteoclast-type giant cells. It occurs in the third to fifth decades of life.

**Pathogenesis:** The neoplastic cells are primitive osteoblast precursors that express high levels of RANKL, promoting the proliferation of osteoclast precursors and their differentiation into mature osteoclasts. This increased activity of osteoclasts is responsible for the tumour being highly lytic and expansile due to uncontrolled bone resorption.
Giant cell tumours develop within the epiphysis and may extend into the metaphysis.
Mostly located near the knee, involving the distal femur or proximal tibia. Although rare, they can metastasise to the lungs but typically regress spontaneously and are rarely fatal.
**Morphology:**

items.text: Grossly, the tumours are large, red-brown masses that frequently undergo cystic degeneration.
Histologically, the tumours consist of uniform oval mononuclear tumour cells and abundant osteoclast-type giant cells with 100 or more nuclei.

**Chondroblastoma (Option A):** is a benign, chondroid-producing tumour that usually arises in the epiphysis or apophysis of skeletally immature individuals. It is characterised by a sheet-like proliferation of chondroblasts and presents with pain, joint stiffness, and swelling. Chondroblastomas rarely show a soap bubble appearance on X-ray.

**Osteosarcoma (Option C):** is a malignant bone tumour, typically found in the metaphysis of long bones. It is most common in children and young adults, particularly around sites of bone growth. It can present with bone pain, swelling, and fractures but does not typically exhibit the soap bubble appearance associated with giant cell tumours.

**Osteochondroma (Option D):** is a benign bone tumour that forms on the surface of bones, usually near the growth plate. It comprises bone and cartilage and tends to stop growing after skeletal maturity. They do not present with a soap bubble appearance and are typically not located in the epiphysis.

blocks.text: Metallosis refers to the accumulation of metal debris in tissues commonly associated with wear and corrosion of metal implants, such as those used in joint replacements. This causes inflammation, foreign body giant cells, and metallic debris, visible on histopathology.
**Metallosis:**

items.text: **Definition:** Aseptic fibrosis, local necrosis, and prosthetic loosening due to metal wear and corrosion in metal-on-metal (MoM) implants.

**Pathophysiology:** Metallic debris (cobalt, chromium, titanium) triggers an inflammatory response, leading to foreign body giant cell reaction, cytokine release, and tissue necrosis. Systemic metal ion absorption may cause neuropathy, cardiomyopathy, and thyroid dysfunction.
**Clinical Features:** Local: Chronic pain, swelling, pseudotumors, skin discolouration. Systemic: Neurological, cardiac, and endocrine toxicity.
**Diagnosis:** Serum cobalt and chromium levels. MARS MRI (Metal Artifact Reduction Sequence) for pseudotumors.
**Histopathology:** Pigmented macrophages, metal debris, necrosis.
**Management:** Regular monitoring of metal ion levels and symptoms. Revision surgery with non-metallic implants in symptomatic cases.

blocks.text: **Incorrect Options:**

items.text: **Ochronosis (Option A):** A rare condition often associated with alkaptonuria, characterized by dark pigmentation in cartilage but not related to metal debris from implants.

**Malignant melanoma (Option C)** is a type of skin cancer that arises from melanocytes. It typically presents as a pigmented skin lesion and does not cause the formation of foreign body giant cells or be associated with metal debris from joint replacements.

**Rosai-Dorfman disease (Option D)** is a rare condition characterized by the accumulation of histiocytes (a type of white blood cell) in various organs, leading to lymphadenopathy and other systemic symptoms. It is not related to the inflammatory response caused by metal debris in metallosis.

blocks.text: Follicular lymphoma is less likely to result in a dry bone marrow aspiration compared to the other conditions. In follicular lymphoma, the bone marrow may be infiltrated with lymphoma cells but typically retains enough cellularity for a successful aspiration.
**Conditions that can lead to a dry bone marrow aspiration (Dry tap):**

items.text: Metastatic carcinoma infiltration (17%)
Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) (15%)
Myelofibrosis (14%)
Hairy cell leukemia (10%)
Acute leukemia (10%)
Lymphomas, including Hodgkin’s disease.

blocks.text: **Hairy Cell Leukemia (HCL) (Option A):** , Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) (Option B) (e.g., AML with myelofibrosis), and Myelodysplastic Syndrome (MDS) (Option C) can all cause dry bone marrow aspiration due to bone marrow fibrosis, increased reticulin deposition or dense cellular infiltration.

Xeroderma pigmentosa is caused by a defect in nucleotide excision repair, leading to an inability to repair UV-induced DNA damage, which results in extreme sensitivity to sunlight and a high risk of skin cancers.
**Incorrect Options:** Options B, C, and D do not cause xeroderma pigmentosa.
The given microscopy image reveals Michaelis Guttman bodies, along with cutaneous malakoplakia on the scalp region.
**Incorrect Options:** Options A, C, and D do not show Michaelis Guttman's bodies.

The histopathological image showing keratin pearls on histopathology is suggestive of Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC). It is a malignant tumour originating from epidermal keratinocytes. It is the second most common skin tumour after basal cell carcinoma (BCC). SCC is notably the most common skin tumour in immunocompromised individuals.
**Predisposing factors** include UV exposure, immunosuppression, and conditions like xeroderma pigmentosum, albinism, LP, and DLE, which can rarely progress into SCC.

**Clinical features:** It typically exhibits a lower rate of local, regional, and distant spread compared to other skin malignancies. Associated with immunocompromised states such as HIV infection and renal transplant recipients.
It presents as papules, nodules, or plaques with induration and signs of photodamage like crusting and scaling. Histopathological examination reveals characteristic keratin pearls.
**Treatment:** Primary treatment involves wide surgical excision with margins. Advanced cases may require radiation or chemotherapy.

items.text: **BCC (Basal Cell Carcinoma) (Option B):** is the most common type of skin cancer, originating from the basal cells in the epidermis. It is typically slow-growing, often appearing as a painless, pearly nodule with telangiectasias on sun-exposed areas like the face. Histologically, BCC is characterised by nests of basaloid cells with a palisading pattern at the periphery, fibrotic stroma, and clefting between the tumour and surrounding tissue.

**Molluscum contagiosum (Option C):** is a viral skin infection causing small, flesh-coloured lesions with central umbilication, often in children and immunocompromised individuals. Histologically, it shows epidermal hyperplasia, ballooning keratinocytes, and Henderson-Patterson (HP) bodies in cup-shaped spaces.

**Verrucous carcinoma (Option D):** is a rare, low-grade squamous cell carcinoma often found in areas with chronic irritation (e.g., oral cavity, genitals). It presents as a slow-growing, wart-like lesion and is associated with HPV infection. Histopathologically, it shows exophytic growth, thick keratinisation, well-differentiated squamous cells, and pushing borders with minimal atypia.

blocks.text: The histopathological image of the skin biopsy reveals nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading and a distinctive stromal retraction artefact, characteristic of Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC), also known as Rodent Ulcer. It is the most common type of skin cancer and is typically seen in sun-exposed areas of the skin. It is a slow-growing, locally invasive tumour, and it rarely metastasises.
**Origin:** Arises from pluripotent cells within the basal layer of the epidermis or follicular structures.
**Pathogenesis:**
**Site:** Face, Around eyes, Nose
**Clinical Features:**

items.text: It presents initially small, scaly plaque.
They present as pearly papules containing dilated blood vessels (telangiectasias)
They may ulcerate locally and invade the underlying bone or facial sinuses (rodent ulcers).
Slow progressive course of peripheral extension.

blocks.text: **Histologically:** The tumour cells are basophilic cells with hyperchromatic nuclei (basaloid cells) arranged in clusters with a palisading pattern. The stroma sometimes retracts from the malignant cells.
**Treatment:**

items.text: **Medical:** Imiquimod, 5-FU,Intralesional interferon α-2b Hedgehog pathway inhibitors:(Vismodegib)
**Surgical:** Mohs micrographic surgery, Done in recurrent BCCs.

**Squamous cell Carcinoma (Option B):** typically exhibits keratin pearls and intercellular bridges, features not present in the image provided. Additionally, the cells are generally larger and have more abundant cytoplasm, unlike the smaller basaloid cells seen in BCC.
**Adenocarcinoma (Option C)** arises from glandular epithelium and shows glandular structures or mucin production.

**Malignant Melanoma (Option D):** is characterised by atypical melanocytes, which can be seen in various configurations, such as nests or single cells within the epidermis and dermis. These cells often contain melanin pigment.

blocks.text: The patient described is likely suffering from Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), a genetic disorder characterised by progressive muscle weakness, particularly in the lower limbs, with pseudohypertrophy of the calf muscles. This condition is caused by a mutation in the dystrophin gene, resulting in the absence or severe deficiency of dystrophin, a protein that helps anchor the muscle cell membrane.

Dystrophin deficient Truncated and unstable (< 3% of normal)

blocks.text: **Incorrect Options:** Abnormal collagen (Option A) would be more consistent with conditions like Ehlers-Danlos syndrome or osteogenesis imperfecta, which involve defective collagen synthesis. Dystrophinopathies, like DMD, do not primarily involve collagen.

items.text: **Expansion of CAG triplet repeats (Option C):** can cause Huntington's disease or fragile X syndrome, but DMD is caused by a mutation in the dystrophin gene, not CAG repeats.

**Defective fibrillin (Option D):** is the cause of Marfan syndrome, which affects connective tissue and is characterized by features like tall stature, long limbs, and aortic dissection, but it is not involved in muscle degeneration like DMD.

blocks.text: The most likely diagnosis is a hypertrophic scar, characterised by a raised scar confined to the original wound boundaries, unlike keloids that extend beyond the wound. It is marked by excess collagen, rapid growth, and the presence of myofibroblasts. Hypertrophic scars tend to regress over time and recur less frequently than keloids.
**Keloid: (Option A)** Scar grows beyond the original wound boundaries and doesn’t regress.

items.text: More common among African Americans.
Develops after deep dermal injuries.

blocks.text: **Exuberant Granulation Tissue: (Option B)** Excessive granulation tissue above skin level. Blocks reepithelialisation (also called "proud flesh"). Requires cauterisation or surgical excision for healing
**Contractures:** Abnormal tightening of the wound and surrounding tissues. Common in palms, soles, and chest. Seen in severe burns, it may impair joint movement.

The histopathological image shows Pemphigus Vulgaris (PV), with intraepidermal cleavage and acantholysis in the suprabasal layer, along with a "row of tombstones" appearance due to the separation of basal keratinocytes at the basement membrane zone. It is the most common chronic autoimmune blistering disease caused by antibodies against desmosomal adhesion proteins.
The target antigens for PV are most commonly Desmoglein 3 and sometimes Desmoglein 1.

items.text: **Clinical features:** Flaccid blisters filled with clear fluid present on normal skin or an erythematous base.
The blisters rupture, producing painful erosion.
Mucosal involvement is a very important and one of the distinguishing features of PV.

blocks.text: **Histopathology:** Intraepidermal cleavage with acantholysis (detached keratinocytes) primarily localized to the suprabasal region.
Separation of basal keratinocytes along the basement membrane zone, resulting in an appearance that resembles a "row of tombstones".

items.text: **Leprosy (Option B)**, also known as Hansen's disease, is a chronic infection caused by Mycobacterium leprae, affecting the skin, peripheral nerves, and mucous membranes. Tuberculous leprosy shows granulomatous lesions similar to tuberculosis, while lepromatous leprosy features lipid-laden macrophages (lepra cells) containing "globi" of acid-fast bacilli.

**Mycosis fungoides (Option C):** is the most common type of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. It presents with a variety of skin lesions, including patches, plaques, and tumours. Histologically, the epidermis and upper dermis are infiltrated by neoplastic T cells, which often have a cerebriform appearance due to marked infolding of the nuclear membrane.

**Visceral leishmaniasis (Option D):** , also known as kala-azar, is a systemic parasitic infection caused by Leishmania species. It is characterized by granulomatous inflammation, phagocytosed parasites, hyperplasia of the reticuloendothelial system, necrosis with fibrosis, and hemophagocytosis, where macrophages engulf red blood cells, white blood cells, or platelets.

blocks.text: The clinical presentation of a 5-year-old child with proptosis and a desmin-positive tumour suggests embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS). Desmin is a marker for muscle differentiation, and rhabdomyosarcoma, a malignant tumour of skeletal muscle origin, is common in children and can present with proptosis if it involves the orbit.
**Rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS):**

items.text: **Origin:** A malignant tumour arising from skeletal muscle progenitors
**Types:** Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma. Alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma. Pleomorphic rhabdomyosarcoma. Spindle cell/sclerosing rhabdomyosarcoma

**Clinical features:** It is the most common soft tissue sarcoma in children and adolescents. It commonly presents in the extremities. Pediatric rhabdomyosarcomas mostly arise in the sinuses, head and neck, and genitourinary tract.
**IHC Positive Markers:** Desmin Myogenin MyoD1 Muscle-specific actin
**Gross appearance:** The tumours are often large, soft, and infiltrative, with areas of necrosis and haemorrhage.
**Microscopy:** Small, round to spindle-shaped cells with hyperchromatic nuclei and scant cytoplasm, sometimes with a myxoid stroma, are also seen.

**Ewing’s sarcoma (Option A):** is a malignant tumour typically affecting bones or soft tissues, often seen in children and adolescents. It is characterized by a specific genetic translocation (t(11;22)) and is usually not associated with desmin positivity, which is more typical of rhabdomyosarcoma. Ewing's sarcoma may cause localized swelling or pain but rarely presents with proptosis unless it involves the orbit or surrounding tissues. It is composed of sheets of uniform, small, round cells with scant cytoplasm that may be clear due to abundant glycogen.

**Leukaemia (Option C):** is a type of cancer that affects the blood and bone marrow, leading to the uncontrolled production of abnormal white blood cells. It typically doesn't present with localized tumours or proptosis. However, in cases of leukemic infiltration of the orbit, proptosis may occur, though it's relatively rare.

**Retinoblastoma (Option D):** is a malignant eye tumour that primarily affects young children, often before the age of 5. While it can cause proptosis due to orbital involvement, it is typically not associated with a desmin-positive tumour. Retinoblastoma usually presents with a white reflex in the pupil (leukocoria) and can cause vision problems or strabismus.

blocks.text: Normal reticulocyte count is 0.5-1.5%. Corrected reticulocyte count (CRC) is the correction for the degree of anaemia, and it's calculated using the following formula.
CRC= Observed reticulocyte count x Patient’s haemoglobin / Standard haemoglobin
Standard hemoglobin for men= 15g/dl; for women=13g/dl
For the the above patient: CRC = 5 x 9 / 15 = 3.0
Significance of Corrected Reticulocyte Count
The corrected reticulocyte count is essential in evaluating anaemia to avoid misleadingly high percentages.
Anaemia decreases RBCs, potentially inflating the reticulocyte percentage without increased erythropoiesis.

The correction adjusts the reticulocyte percentage relative to the reduced RBC count, providing a more accurate assessment of bone marrow response. An increased corrected reticulocyte count indicates effective erythropoiesis. Low reticulocyte production may suggest bone marrow issues, iron, vitamin B12, or folate deficiencies.
Primary Sites of Erythropoiesis

items.text: 1st trimester: Yolksac (Option C)
2nd trimester onwards: Liver (Option D)
Children: Bone marrow of almost all bones (Option B)
Adults: Only in the bone marrow of the long bones (e.g., femur, tibia), as well as in the pelvis, vertebrae, and sternum.

blocks.text: The presence of anaemia typically triggers the body's response by increasing erythropoiesis, releasing reticulocytes into circulation early as part of the compensatory mechanism to replenish red blood cells and enhance tissue oxygenation.
New Methylene blue is used to visualise reticulocytes in peripheral blood smears. It is a supravital stain that stains living states like the RNA in reticulocytes.
It picks up RNA as a bluish reticulated network within erythrocytes. This stain is useful in assessing bone marrow function and erythropoietic activity.

**Prussian blue (Option A):** Prussian blue stain detects iron in hemosiderin-containing cells. Iron is chemically reactive and turns blue-black when exposed to potassium ferrocyanide, which is present in Prussian blue.
**PAS Stain (Option C):** A periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stain detects polysaccharides, such as glycogen, glycoproteins, glycolipids, and mucin in tissues.

**Wright's stain (Option D):** Wright’s stain is a mixture of eosin (red) and methylene blue dyes. It is used in blood smears and bone marrow aspirates to detect RBCs, WBCs, and Platelets abnormalities.
Reticulocytes are smaller pyknotic cells with increased haemoglobin content and have no nucleus.
Increased RBC production occurs as a compensatory mechanism in anaemia, initiating erythropoiesis, which is stimulated by the release of erythropoietin from the kidneys.

Erythropoietin prompts bone marrow to increase red blood cell production by promoting the proliferation and differentiation of hematopoietic stem cells into erythroid progenitor cells, ultimately leading to the maturation of red blood cells.
Stages of Erythropoiesis
It starts with Hematopoietic stem cells(HSC)→Common Myeloid Progenitor cells(CMP)→Proerythroblasts.
Once the proerythroblast has been formed, it divides multiple times, eventually forming many mature RBCs.

items.text: **Proerythroblast-** first cell in which Hb is visualised on Electron microscopy.
**Intermediate normoblast-** first cell in which Hb is visualised on Light microscopy.

blocks.text: The first-generation cells are called basophil erythroblasts because they stain with basic dyes.

Haemoglobin first appears in polychromatophilic erythroblasts and progressively increases. As erythropoiesis progresses, the cell and nucleus size progressively decreases. The reticulocyte is the first cell without a nucleus.
During the reticulocyte stage, the cells pass from the bone marrow into the blood capillaries by diapedesis (squeezing through the pores of the capillary membrane).
factors affecting erythropoiesis

items.text: increasing- EPO, Growth hormone, T3, Cortisol, Testosterone
decreasing- estrogen

blocks.text: Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML) is a myeloproliferative neoplasm characterised by the presence of the Philadelphia chromosome, resulting in the abnormal proliferation of myeloid cells. The marrow in CML is hypercellular due to increased numbers of maturing granulocytic precursors (promyelocytes, myelocytes, eosinophils and basophils).
A characteristic finding is the presence of scattered macrophages with abundant wrinkled, green-blue cytoplasm (sea-blue histiocytes).
CML can lead to increased cellularity in the bone marrow, it typically does not cause significant fibrosis or hypocellularity, the primary factor contributing to dry taps.
**Causes of Dry Tap:**

items.text: Aplastic anaemia
Hairy cell Leukemia
Myelofibrosis
Myelophthisic anaemia
AML-M7

blocks.text: Bone marrow biopsy (instead of BM aspiration) will be helpful in these conditions.
The expected percentage of cellularity in a bone marrow biopsy can be estimated using the formula: % Cellularity =100 − age of the patient
So, for a 45-year-old person: Cellularity = 100 − 45 = 55%
Therefore, the expected percentage of cellularity in their bone marrow biopsy would be 55%.
This ratio tends to be more evenly distributed in adults, with around 50% of each cell type present. (1:1) (Option A)
Two primary constituents Within the bone marrow are hematopoietic and fat cells.

A child's marrow typically consists of 75% hematopoietic cells and 25% fat cells (3:1) (Option D), contrasting with an elderly individual's marrow, which contains approximately 25% hematopoietic and 75% fat cells (1:3). (Option B)
These proportions vary with age and health conditions, illustrating the dynamic nature of bone marrow composition.
The Jamshidi Needle (T-shaped needle) is the most commonly used needle for bone marrow aspiration and biopsy due to its design, which allows for minimal trauma and obtaining an intact core biopsy.
**Salah needle (Option A):** This needle is used for only bone marrow aspiration and not for biopsy.

**Klima needle (Option B):** The Klima needle is also used for bone marrow aspiration. It functions similarly to the Salah needle in aspirating bone marrow cells but is not the primary tool for obtaining a core biopsy
**Quincke needle (Option D):** The Quincke needle is used primarily for lumbar puncture procedures (spinal taps) to collect cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). It is not used for bone marrow biopsies.

MCHC indicates the amount of haemoglobin per unit volume. In contrast to MCH, MCHC correlates the haemoglobin content with the volume of the cells. It is expressed as g/dl of red blood cells or as a percentage value.
MCHC (g/dl) = Hb x 100/ PCV or Hematocrit
Given: Hemoglobin (Hb) = 15 g/dL; Hematocrit (Hct) = 45%
Using the formula for MCHC: MCHC(g/dL)=Hemoglobin (g/dL)×100/Hematocrit (%)

blocks.text: MCH (Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin) measures the average amount of haemoglobin per red blood cell, expressed in picograms (pg) per cell. MCH provides important information about the hemoglobin content in individual red blood cells, which is crucial for diagnosing and classifying types of anemia.
MCH (pg) = Hb x 10/ RBC count
Given: Hemoglobin (Hb) = 14 g/dL; RBC count = 4.7 million cells/μL
Using the formula for MCH: MCH(pg)=Hemoglobin (g/dL)×10/RBC count (millions/μL)

blocks.text: The mean corpuscular volume (MCV) is a critical measurement to identify the underlying cause of anaemia. MCV is a laboratory value that measures the average size and volume of red blood cells expressed as femtoliters (fL). It provides essential information in the diagnostic process for anaemia. To calculate the MCV value, the per cent hematocrit is divided by the erythrocyte count and multiplied by 10.
MCV (fL) = PCV x 10/ RBC count
Given: RBC count: 4.5 million cells/μL; Hematocrit/ PCV: 40%

blocks.text: **Purpose of Methemoglobin Reduction Test:** Used to detect glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. Measures the ability of red blood cells to convert methemoglobin back to hemoglobin. Helps assess the enzymatic activity crucial for protecting cells from oxidative stress.

**Mechanism in G6PD Deficiency:** Individuals with G6PD deficiency have reduced enzyme activity. Red blood cells are more vulnerable to oxidative damage. Impaired reduction of methemoglobin indicates decreased G6PD function.

**Testing Procedure:** The blood sample is exposed to a chemical that induces methemoglobin formation. The rate of reduction back to hemoglobin is measured. The slower reduction compared to normal suggests G6PD deficiency.

**Clinical Application:** Used to confirm diagnosis in patients suspected of having G6PD deficiency. Helps guide management decisions in conditions where oxidative stress can trigger hemolysis. Provides insight into the enzymatic function critical for maintaining red blood cell integrity.

blocks.text: The given clinical scenario and peripheral smear showing spherocytes most likely suggest a diagnosis of hereditary spherocytosis. Hereditary spherocytosis (HS) is an inherited disorder caused by intrinsic defects in the red cell membrane skeleton that render red cells spheroid, less deformable, and vulnerable to splenic sequestration and destruction.
It has an autosomal dominant inheritance(75%) characterized by ankyrin mutation and an autosomal recessive inheritance characterized by spectrin mutation.

**Pathophysiology of hereditary spherocytosis:** The most specific morphologic finding is spherocytosis: Dark-staining (hyperchromic) spherocytes lacking the central zone of pallor. Other features include reticulocytosis.

The characteristic clinical features are anemia, splenomegaly, jaundice, and an increased risk of gallstones. Severity ranges from asymptomatic to severe hemolytic anemia requiring transfusions. Early complications include neonatal jaundice and hemolytic crises. Late complications include gallstones and rarely iron overload.

Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency is an X-linked recessive disorder characterised by a deficiency in the G6PD enzyme, which protects red blood cells from oxidative damage.
This reduces the ability to generate NADPH via the pentose phosphate pathway and impairs glutathione regeneration, exacerbating oxidative stress and hemolysis. (Option B)

When exposed to oxidative stressors, there is an imbalance between the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and antioxidants that neutralize them. This leads to oxidative damage to red blood cell membranes and proteins, resulting in hemolysis. (Option C)

It presents with episodes of acute hemolytic anemia triggered by oxidative stressors such as infections, certain medications (e.g., antimalarials, sulfonamides), or ingestion of certain foods (e.g., fava beans). (Option D)
Clinical manifestations include fatigue, pallor, jaundice, and dark urine (due to hemoglobinuria).

The severity of hemolysis varies depending on the degree of enzyme deficiency and the magnitude of the oxidative insult, with some individuals experiencing life-threatening hemolytic crises. G6PD deficiency causes both intra and extravascular hemolysis.

blocks.text: A black line visible only in the test tubes containing blood sample mixed with a 0.36 buffered solution is suggestive of a positive Nestrof test. The Nestrof test, also known as the Naked Eye Single Tube Red Cell Osmotic Fragility Test, is a screening test used to identify carriers of beta thalassemia and sickle cell anemia.
The test is based on the principle that red blood cells (RBCs) from individuals with beta thalassemia have red blood cells that are more fragile and burst more easily in hypotonic solutions.
**Procedure:**

items.text: Bloood sample is mixed with 0.36% saline solution
After incubation, observe the test tube against a black line. Look for the presence or absence of a black line behind the tube.

blocks.text: **Interpretation:**

items.text: **Positive Test:** Black line visible in only the test tube. A positive NESTROFT indicates that red cells in the tested sample have undergone lysis in 0.36% buffered saline. Thus a positive NESTROFT indicates increased red cell osmotic fragility.
**Negative Test (Normal Result):** No black line visible in any of the test tubes. This indicates that the RBCs have remained intact in control as well as test tube.

blocks.text: Sickle cell disease is a hemoglobinopathy caused by a missense point mutation in the 6th position of the β-globin chain

Therefore they have less severe disease than their homozygous counterparts who have more HbS.
HbF inhibits HbS polymerization more effectively than HbA, keeping infants with sickle cell disease asymptomatic until 5-6 months when HbF levels decline.

Metabolically active intracellular parasites consume oxygen and decrease intracellular pH, promoting sickling of HbAS red cells, which are then rapidly cleared by splenic and hepatic phagocytes, reducing parasite loads. In individuals with coexistent α-thalassemia, reduced Hb synthesis results in milder disease.

Genetic defects in thalassemia involve mutations, insertions, or deletions in the genes responsible for producing hemoglobin chains This results in either decreased or absent production of alpha or beta-globin chains. These defects are inherited in an autosomal recessive manner, meaning an individual must inherit mutated alleles from both parents to manifest the disorder. There are two main types: alpha-thalassemia and beta-thalassemia.

items.text: **1. Alpha-thalassemia:** Resulting from deletions or mutations in the alpha-globin genes located on chromosome 16.
**2. Beta-thalassemia:** Arising from mutations in the beta-globin gene located on chromosome 11.

items.text: **Beta-thalassemia minor (trait):** Reduced beta-globin chain production due to mutations in one allele of the HBB gene.
**Beta-thalassemia major:** Mutations in both alleles of the HBB gene, leading to severe anemia requiring lifelong transfusions and treatment.
**Thalassemia intermedia:** Milder variants and unusual forms of β-thalassemia, also include alpha globin defects in some cases. But the cases does not require regular blood transfusions

Beta-thalassemia mutations are diverse and can occur throughout the HBB gene, which encodes the beta-globin subunit of hemoglobin.

These mutations can affect various aspects of beta-globin production, including transcription, splicing, mRNA stability, and translation. Common types of mutations include point mutations, small insertions or deletions, large deletions, and rearrangements within the HBB gene.
These mutations disrupt normal hemoglobin synthesis, leading to reduced or absent beta-globin production and the characteristic clinical features of beta-thalassemia.

The Prussian blue stain is a histological stain used primarily to detect ferric iron (Fe³⁺) in tissues, cells, and blood smears. It works based on the reaction of potassium ferrocyanide with ferric ions to form an insoluble blue compound called Prussian blue (ferroferric cyanide) which stains blue and is insoluble in water.
The reaction can be summarized as follows:
Fe 3+ + Fe 2+ (Ferrocyanide) ➡ Fe 3 (Fe(CN) 6 ) 2
Therefore, when tissues or cells are stained with Prussian blue, ferric iron deposits appear blue under microscopy, aiding in the detection and localization of iron in biological specimens.
**Note:** Lillie’s stain is used for ferrous (Fe 2+ ) detection.

blocks.text: Microcytosis (smaller than normal red cells) and hypochromia are classic findings in iron deficiency anemia, which is consistent with the patient's symptoms and low hemoglobin. In iron deficiency anemia (IDA), a peripheral blood smear can reveal characteristic changes.

items.text: **Hypochromic Red Blood Cells:** The RBCs appear pale due to decreased hemoglobin content.

blocks.text: In iron deficiency anemia, ferritin translation is decreased by binding iron regulatory protein to iron response elements.
**Iron regulatory mechanism:**

items.text: **IRP:** Binds to IREs in specific mRNAs' untranslated regions (UTRs) to control the translation of proteins involved in iron metabolism.
**IRE:** These are sequences found in the mRNAs of proteins involved in iron metabolism, such as ferritin and transferrin receptor 1
**Ferritin:** Ferritin stores iron inside cells. When iron levels are low, IRPs bind to IREs in the 5' UTR of ferritin mRNA, preventing its translation to conserve iron.

**Transferrin receptor 1 (TfR1):** TfR1 imports iron into cells. When iron levels are low, IRPs bind to IREs in the 3' UTR of TfR1 mRNA, stabilizing it and increasing its translation to enhance iron uptake.

blocks.text: DMT-1 is a transmembrane protein that facilitates the transport of divalent metal ions, primarily ferrous iron (Fe 2+ ), across the apical membrane of enterocytes in the duodenum. Heme iron enters the intestinal cells directly through a heme transporter. Non-heme iron (Fe³⁺) is first reduced to Fe²⁺ by duodenal cytochrome B, then Fe²⁺ enters the cells via the DMT-1 transporter (Option C).
Inside the duodenal cell, Fe²⁺ can either be stored as mucosal iron or transported into the bloodstream.

items.text: **Fe²⁺ exits the cell through ferroportin (Option A):**

**The liver secretes hepcidin (Option D):** a protein that regulates iron absorption. When iron stores are adequate, hepcidin downregulates ferroportin expression, reducing iron absorption.

blocks.text: Basophilic stippling is a characteristic finding seen in lead poisoning. items.text: **Schistocytes (Option A):** These fragmented red blood cells are typically seen in microangiopathic hemolytic anaemia caused by conditions such as thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) or disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), not in lead poisoning.

blocks.text: The peripheral blood smear shows enlarged oval-shaped red blood cells (macro-ovalocytes) with hyperchromia and hypersegmented neutrophils. This suggests megaloblastic anaemia, which in this scenario would be due to folate deficiency caused by methotrexate.
Common causes of folate deficiency are given below:

items.text: **Decreased intake:** Inadequate diet. Alcoholism. Infancy.
**Impaired absorption:** Malabsorption states. Intrinsic intestinal disease. Anticonvulsants, oral contraceptives.
**Increased loss:** Haemodialysis.
**Increased requirement:** Pregnancy. Infancy. Disseminated cancer. Markedly increased hematopoiesis.
**Impaired utilisation:** Folic acid antagonists (Methotrexate).

blocks.text: Plasma and urinary methylmalonic acid levels will be elevated in case of vitamin B12 deficiency but not with folate deficiency. This is because the enzyme methylmalonyl coenzyme A mutase's isomerisation of methylmalonyl coenzyme A to succinyl coenzyme A requires adenosylcobalamin (a form of vitamin B12) as a cofactor. A deficiency of vitamin B12 thus leads to increased plasma and urine levels of methylmalonic acid.

items.text: Vitamin B12 is key in converting homocysteine to methionine; hence, its deficiency will lead to elevated homocysteine levels (Option A) rather than reduction.
Neurological symptoms will remain the same, if not worsen, after folate administration in case of Vitamin B12 deficient megaloblastic anaemia (Option B).

blocks.text: Improvement in symptoms and reduction in megaloblastic count occur after folate administration, even if the anaemia is due to Vitamin B12 deficiency (Option D).

Elevated urinary levels of formiminoglutamic acid (FIGlu) in a patient to whom histidine is given suggests the presence of folic acid deficiency. This is called the FIGlu test. Folic acid is normally required in its tetrahydrofolate form to regulate DNA synthesis and the production of methionine, glutamate, etc. Formiminoglutamic acid derived from histidine will be converted to glutamate in the presence of folic acid.
If there is a folic acid deficiency, this conversion will not occur, leading to elevated urinary formiminoglutamic acid.
**Presence of antibodies against intrinsic factor (Option A):** Antibodies to intrinsic factor will be seen in pernicious anaemia in which there will be vitamin B12 deficiency.
**Neurological symptoms are common (Option C):** Neurological symptoms will be seen in Vitamin B12 deficiency, not folate deficiency.

This patient’s symptoms with a history of poor dietary habits and laboratory findings of Hb 9 g/dL with an MCV of 80 fl (microcytic anaemia) strongly suggest iron deficiency anaemia. Iron deficiency anaemia can result from dietary lack, impaired absorption, increased iron requirement (e.g., during pregnancy), or chronic blood loss (e.g., gastrointestinal bleeding).
Clinical features include Koilonychia, alopecia, atrophic glossitis, esophageal webs, pica and intestinal malabsorption, affecting overall nutritional status.
**Cyanocobalamin deficiency (Option A):** causes megaloblastic anemia, which typically presents with macrocytic anemia (elevated MCV), not the microcytic anemia seen in this patient.
**Folic acid deficiency (Option B):** also causes megaloblastic anemia, which presents with macrocytic anemia (high MCV), not microcytic anemia.
**Hereditary spherocytosis (Option D):** is a condition where red blood cells are abnormally shaped (spherocytes), leading to hemolysis and normocytic anemia (normal MCV).

The next investigation of choice for a child suspected to have Chloroma (also known as Granulocytic Sarcoma or Myeloblastoma) is a bone marrow biopsy. It is a localized extramedullary myeloid tumour composed of immature myeloid cells, which can occur in patients with acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) or myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS). It is not a benign tumour, but it has a greenish colour.
**Site:** Soft tissue involvement in orbit leads to proptosis.
Associated with AML M2 and M5.
**Bone marrow biopsy:** Confirms the diagnosis by revealing the presence of abnormal myeloid cells infiltrating the bone marrow. (Option D)
**Peripheral smear findings:** Myeloblasts.
**Arbiskov cells:** Atypical monocytes/macrophages.
**Markers:** MPO (green colour), CD 43, CD 45 and Lysozyme.
**Platelet count (Option A):** , WBC count (Option B) and Flow cytometry (Option C) might be done but they do not confirm the diagnosis of chloroma.
1 & 2 statements are correct regarding Glucose-6-phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD) Deficiency.
It is an X-linked recessive disorder.

**Pathogenesis:** It is characterized by a deficiency in the G6PD enzyme, which protects red blood cells from oxidative damage. This reduces the ability to generate NADPH (Statement 2) via the pentose phosphate pathway and impairs glutathione regeneration (Statement 1), exacerbating oxidative stress and hemolysis.
When exposed to oxidative stressors, there is an imbalance between the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and antioxidants that neutralize them.
This leads to oxidative damage to red blood cell membranes and proteins, resulting in hemolysis. (Statement 4)
**Clinical features:**

items.text: Episodes of acute hemolytic anaemia triggered by oxidative stressors such as infections, certain medications (e.g., antimalarials, sulfonamides), or ingestion of certain foods (e.g., fava beans).
Fatigue, pallor, jaundice, and dark urine (due to hemoglobinuria).

blocks.text: The severity of hemolysis varies depending on the degree of enzyme deficiency and the magnitude of the oxidative insult, with some individuals experiencing life-threatening hemolytic crises.
G6PD deficiency causes both intra and extravascular hemolysis.
**Decreased lipid peroxidation (Statement 3):** G6PD deficiency does not directly lead to a reduction in lipid peroxidation.

On the contrary, it can increase susceptibility to oxidative stress and the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS). The reduced levels of NADPH and glutathione in G6PD deficiency impair the cell's antioxidant defence mechanisms, resulting in enhanced lipid peroxidation and oxidative damage.
The treatment of Sideroblastic Anemia involves the use of vitamin B6 (pyridoxine).

**Sideroblastic Anemia:** It is a condition characterized by defective heme synthesis in the bone marrow, leading to the accumulation of iron within the mitochondria of red blood cell precursors (sideroblasts).
**Causes**
**Congenital causes:** Due to enzyme deficiencies like ALA synthase, ferrochelatase, etc.
**Acquired causes**

items.text: Vitamin B6 deficiency
Drugs like isoniazid and chloramphenicol
Lead and alcohol poisoning

blocks.text: **Pathogenesis:** Vitamin B6 is crucial for the proper function of enzymes in heme synthesis. As a cofactor for aminolevulinic acid synthase, it aids in the first step of heme production. Ensuring sufficient vitamin B6 restores enzyme activity, supports heme synthesis, and helps alleviate symptoms of sideroblastic anaemia.
**Microscopy**
**Peripheral Smear: Pappenheimer bodies:** Multiple basophilic iron aggregates. Stain blue with Perl's/ Prussian blue. Seen in sideroblastic anaemia, lead poisoning, or hemochromatosis.

**Bone Marrow: Ringed Sideroblasts:** Blue granules form a full or partial ring. Blasts have a nucleus. Iron is present in mitochondria in the perinuclear region. Stain blue on Perl's/Prussian blue. Seen with Sideroblastic anemia and Myelodysplastic syndrome.
**Associated with SF3B1 mutation**

**Vitamin B1 (Option C):** , or thiamine, plays a key role in carbohydrate metabolism and nerve function. Its deficiency causes conditions like Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome and Beriberi, but it is not linked to sideroblastic anaemia.

**Vitamin B12 (Option A):** deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia and neurological symptoms. It results from poor diet, malabsorption, or lack of intrinsic factors. In sideroblastic anaemia, vitamin B6 is used instead of vitamin B12 because it helps correct the heme synthesis defect, while B12 is not involved in this process.

**Iron (Option D):** deficiency presents with symptoms like pale skin, shortness of breath, dizziness or lightheadedness, brittle nails, headaches, restless legs syndrome, etc. In sideroblastic anaemia, treatment focuses on addressing the underlying cause, as the main issue is impaired heme synthesis. Iron supplementation is generally ineffective and may worsen the condition by increasing iron accumulation in tissues.

Transferrin saturation is decreased in iron deficiency anaemia. This is because although TIBC is elevated, there is not enough iron to saturate the transferrin molecules, leading to low transferrin saturation.
**Iron Study Interpretation in Iron Deficiency Anemia:**

items.text: **Serum Ferritin:** Low (< 30 ng/mL)
**Serum Iron (Fe):** Low
**Serum transferrin saturation (Option A):** Low
**Total Iron Binding Capacity (TIBC) (Option C ruled out):** Increased: TIBC reflects the increased capacity of transferrin to bind iron in response to low iron stores.
**Red Cell Distribution Width (RDW):** Increased
**Ferritin soluble receptors (sTfR) (Option D ruled out):** Increased
**RBC protoporphyrin (Option B ruled out):** Increased
**Bone Marrow Aspiration and Iron Staining:** Confirmatory test for Iron deficiency anaemia.

blocks.text: The clinical presentation of gum bleeding, fever, pallor, severe anaemia, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia, along with the findings of peripheral smear and bone marrow biopsy, strongly point toward idiopathic acquired aplastic anaemia (AAA).
**Aplastic Anemia** is characterised by bone marrow failure, where the bone marrow does not produce enough blood cells, leading to Pancytopenia.

In severe cases, the bone marrow may become hypocellular, making it difficult to aspirate sufficient material, leading to a dry tap. The absence of immature cells and the presence of fatty streaks in the bone marrow suggests bone marrow failure, typical of aplastic anemia, where normal hematopoiesis is replaced by fat.

**Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (Option B):** is a rare disorder that causes red blood cells to prematurely break down by the complement system. It is characterised by hemolytic anemia and hemoglobinuria. The peripheral smear shows evidence of hemolysis, which is not the case here.

**Myelodysplastic syndrome (Option C):** is a group of disorders characterised by ineffective hematopoiesis and dysplastic cells in the bone marrow. While MDS can cause pancytopenia, it would typically show dysplastic features in the marrow, including abnormal shapes of cells, which is not the case here.

**Tuberculosis (Option D):** is an infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis that is not commonly associated with severe pancytopenia, fatty marrow, or absence of megakaryocytes. TB-related bone marrow suppression would usually have other findings like granulomas.
In iron deficiency anaemia, ferritin translation is decreased by binding iron regulatory protein to iron response elements.
**Iron regulatory mechanism:**

items.text: **IRP:** Binds to IREs in specific mRNAs' untranslated regions (UTRs) to control the translation of proteins involved in iron metabolism.
**IRE:** These are sequences found in the mRNAs of proteins involved in iron metabolism, such as ferritin and transferrin receptor 1
**Ferritin:** Ferritin stores iron inside cells. When iron levels are low, IRPs bind to IREs in the 5' UTR of ferritin mRNA, preventing its translation to conserve iron.
**Transferrin receptor 1 (TfR1):** TfR1 imports iron into cells.

blocks.text: When intracellular iron levels are low, IRP binds to the IRE in the ferritin mRNA, preventing its translation. This leads to a decrease in the production of ferritin, which helps conserve iron and prevent its storage when it is limited.

**Ferritin translation is increased by binding IRP to IRE (Option A):** In iron deficiency anaemia, the binding of IRP to the IRE in the mRNA of ferritin leads to a decrease in ferritin translation to conserve iron and prevents its storage when it is limited.

**Transferrin receptor 1 translation is unaffected by binding IRP to IRE (Option C):** In iron deficiency, IRP binds to the IRE in the mRNA of TfR1, stabilizing the mRNA and increasing its translation, resulting in an increased production of TfR1, which enhances the uptake of iron into cells to compensate for the deficiency.

**Transferrin receptor 1 translation is decreased by binding IRP to IRE (Option D):** In iron deficiency anaemia, the binding of IRP to the IRE in the mRNA of TfR1 leads to an increased translation of TfR1, facilitating the increased uptake of iron into cells to overcome the deficiency.

items.text: Neutrophils are granulocytes with a multilobed nucleus and pale cytoplasm containing fine pinkish granules. They are the most abundant white blood cells and play a key role in innate immunity through phagocytosis and enzyme release.
Lymphocytes have a large, round nucleus, a small amount of cytoplasm & no granules.
Monocytes are the largest cells with a kidney-shaped nucleus and a substantial cytoplasm.
Eosinophils are granulocytes with a bilobed nucleus and prominent brick-red granules in their cytoplasm.
Basophils are a type of granulocyte with a segmented nucleus and large bluish granules in their cytoplasm.

blocks.text: Stem cells can differentiate into various cell types, replicate, and regenerate damaged tissues.

However, they do not divide uncontrollably or without regulatory stimuli. Their division is tightly regulated by signalling pathways to ensure proper function and prevent uncontrolled cell proliferation, which could lead to issues like cancer.
**Stem cells:**

items.text: **Dual property:** Stem cells can self-renew (Option B) and differentiate (Option A) into various cell types.
**Totipotent stem cells:** Found during development, can generate all cell types in the body.
**Adult stem cells:** Present in tissues, maintain cell populations, and repair damage (Option D). Limited differentiation capacity, typically producing cells within their respective tissues.

blocks.text: **Main types:**

items.text: **Embryonic stem (ES) cells:** Totipotent, can differentiate into all cell types.
**Adult (Tissue) stem cells:** Limited to differentiating into specific tissue types, regulated by stem cell niches.

blocks.text: **Examples:**

items.text: **Hematopoietic stem cells:** Replenish blood cells in bone marrow, used in clinical treatments like leukaemia.
**Mesenchymal stem cells:** Found in bone marrow and fat, they can differentiate into stromal cells (cartilage, bone, fat, muscle) and aid tissue regeneration.

blocks.text: In glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, oxidative stress leads to the formation of bite cells (also called degmacytes) due to the removal of damaged portions of the cell membrane.
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency is an inherited enzyme affecting red blood cells. Caused by a lack of the G6PD enzyme, which protects red blood cells from oxidative damage.

Oxidative stress makes red blood cells vulnerable, leading to hemolysis. A characteristic feature is the presence of bite cells (degmacytes). Heinz bodies, formed from denatured haemoglobin, are not visible with Romanowsky stains. When Romanowsky stains are used, the denatured haemoglobin may not be detected, resulting in the appearance of bite cells.

rows: Oxidative stress leads to cross-linking of sulfhydryl groups in haemoglobin → Denaturation of haemoglobin → Heinz bodies. RBCs with Heinz bodies pass through the spleen → Splenic macrophages try to pluck these Heinz bodies → Membrane loss → Bite cells.

↓ Haemoglobin content in RBCs → ↓ RBC volume → Surface area relatively unchanged → ↑ Surface area to volume ratio→ Altered lipid composition → ↑ Formation of membrane protrusions→ ↑ Membrane instability → ↓ Hemoglobin accumulation in certain membrane areas → Central area with haemoglobin, clear zone, outer ring. Uneven distribution of haemoglobin and lipids → Characteristic "bull's-eye" appearance of Target cells
Abnormal Hemoglobin (HbS) → HbS molecules polymerize under low oxygen → RBCs become rigid and assume a sickle shape.
Genetic defect in RBC membrane protein(spectrin) • Loss of membrane surface area • RBCs become spherical.

blocks.text: **Spectrin defect (Option A):** is a structural protein that maintains the shape and flexibility of red blood cells. Deficiency of spectrin is seen in hereditary spherocytosis, not G6PD deficiency.
**Cells do not lyse in hypotonic solution (Option C):** In G6PD deficiency, red blood cells are more likely to lyse in hypotonic solutions due to their increased vulnerability to oxidative stress.

**Cells lyse in hypertonic solution (Option D):** Red blood cells do not typically lyse in hypertonic solutions; instead, they undergo crenation. The lysis occurs more readily in hypotonic solutions, especially in G6PD deficiency.

blocks.text: **Aplastic anaemia (Option A)** is a condition where the bone marrow fails to produce enough blood cells, resulting in a reduction of red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets.
**Vitamin B12 deficiency (Option B):** leads to megaloblastic anaemia and is often accompanied by neurological symptoms such as numbness and tingling.
**Hypoalbuminemia (Option D):** is characterized by low blood albumin levels. It is associated with Muehrcke's lines, which appear as paired, narrow white bands on the fingernails.

In polycythemia vera (>95% cases), the JAK2 mutation leads to the persistent activation of the JAK-STAT signalling pathway, resulting in the uncontrolled proliferation and survival of red blood cell precursors. This overproduction increases red blood cell count in the bloodstream, leading to blood thickening and potential complications like thrombosis.

items.text: **Essential thrombocytosis (Option B):** is characterized by the overproduction of platelets in the bone marrow, increasing the risk of abnormal blood clotting. Although JAK2 mutations can occur in essential thrombocytosis, they are less frequent compared to polycythemia vera.

**Chronic myelogenous leukaemia (CML) (Option C):** is primarily associated with the Philadelphia chromosome, which results from a reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22. This translocation leads to the creation of the BCR-ABL fusion gene, which causes uncontrolled proliferation of myeloid cells.

**Primary myelofibrosis (PMF) (Option D):** involves the excessive production of abnormal blood cells, often leading to fibrosis (scarring) of the bone marrow. JAK2 mutations can also occur in primary myelofibrosis, though they are less common than in polycythemia vera.

blocks.text: Clot activator is found in red-top vacutainer tubes and is used to promote blood clotting, which is needed for serum separation in various tests.

Vitamin B12 deficiency is commonly associated with macrocytic anemia, which is characterized by the presence of macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils on the peripheral blood smears. It can be caused by atrophic gastritis, which leads to impaired absorption of B12 due to reduced intrinsic factor production. Atrophic gastritis is frequently seen in pernicious anemia, a common cause of vitamin B12 deficiency.

blocks.text: **Folate deficiency (Option B)** can cause macrocytic anemia and hypersegmented neutrophils.
However, it is less commonly associated with atrophic gastritis, and the absence of other features like neural tube defects (in pregnancy) makes it less likely in this case.
**Pyridoxine deficiency (Option C):** (Vitamin B6) deficiency causes microcytic anemia and not macrocytic anemia and is unlikely to explain the findings of macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils.

**Niacin deficiency (Option D):** (Vitamin B3) deficiency causes pellagra, which is characterised by the "three D's": dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia. It does not cause macrocytic anemia or hypersegmented neutrophils.

The patient presents with macrocytic anemia (MCV = 101 fL) and peripheral smear findings of macrocytic RBCs and hypersegmented neutrophils, which strongly indicate megaloblastic anemia. This condition is most commonly caused by deficiencies in vitamin B12 or folate, often due to poor dietary intake, malabsorption, or chronic alcohol use.

Chronic alcohol consumption is a well-known cause of macrocytic anemia, either due to direct toxic effects on hematopoiesis or through the development of folate deficiency, a key cause of megaloblastic anemia.

items.text: **Lead poisoning (Option A):** typically causes microcytic anemia due to interference with heme synthesis.
**Iron deficiency anemia (Option B):** is characterised by microcytic, hypochromic anaemia resulting from reduced haemoglobin production.

**Hemolytic anemia (Option C):** may cause mild macrocytosis due to increased reticulocyte production; hypersegmented neutrophils are not seen. The hallmark findings of hemolysis (e.g., jaundice, reticulocytosis) are absent in this case.

blocks.text: Thalassemia Major (β-Thalassemia Major)

rows: A severe form of β-thalassemia caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the β-globin gene (HBB) on chromosome 11, leading to absent or markedly reduced β-globin chain production.
Autosomal recessive disorder, caused by mutations in the β-globin gene leading to defective hemoglobin synthesis.
Reduced or absent β-globin chains lead to excess α-globin chains, which form unstable precipitates, causing ineffective erythropoiesis, hemolysis, and severe anaemia.

Symptoms appear around 6 months of age (as fetal haemoglobin declines); severe anaemia, growth retardation, hepatosplenomegaly, skeletal deformities (crew-cut appearance on skull X-ray, frontal bossing), jaundice, and delayed puberty.

Peripheral smear: Microcytic hypochromic anaemia, target cells, anisopoikilocytosis, nucleated RBCs.
Bone marrow: Erythroid hyperplasia with expansion of marrow cavities.
Absent or very low HbA, markedly increased HbF (>90%), variable HbA2.

Iron overload (due to repeated transfusions leading to secondary hemochromatosis)
Cardiac failure (due to iron deposition)
E ndocrinopathies (diabetes, hypothyroidism, hypogonadism)
Osteopenia/osteoporosis
Increased infection risk (especially from Yersinia and viral infections).

Blood tests (CBC, peripheral smear), Hb electrophoresis/HPLC, Serum ferritin (for iron overload), Genetic testing (HBB gene mutations), Prenatal diagnosis (chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis).

Regular blood transfusions, iron chelation therapy (deferoxamine, deferasirox, deferiprone), splenectomy (in refractory cases), and hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) (only curative option).
Carrier screening, genetic counselling, prenatal diagnosis, preimplantation genetic diagnosis (PGD) in high-risk couples.

blocks.text: The Mentzer index (MCV/RBC count) helps distinguish IDA from beta-thalassemia minor, with a value <13 suggesting beta-thalassemia minor. An elevated RDW favours IDA in microcytic, hypochromic anaemia.
Confirmatory test: Hemoglobin electrophoresis showing HbA₂ >3.5% confirms beta-thalassemia minor.
**Megaloblastic anaemia (Option A):** The main causes are folate and vitamin B12 deficiency.
Peripheral blood shows hypersegmented neutrophils and macroovalocytes as early changes. Bone marrow is hypercellular, with numerous megaloblasts and giant metamyelocytes.

**Iron deficiency anemia (Option B):** is the most common nutritional deficiency in the world. Diagnostic criteria include anaemia, hypochromic and microcytic red cell indices, low serum ferritin and iron levels, low transferrin saturation, and increased total iron-binding capacity.
**Pernicious anaemia (Option D):** The most common cause of vitamin B12 deficiency, resulting from autoimmune destruction of gastric mucosa, leading to intrinsic factor deficiency.

The clinical presentation of a young boy from a high altitude with fever, weakness, high hemoglobin, and increased TLC with a predominance of neutrophils and myeloid cells suggests reactive or secondary polycythemia. In this context, it is important to assess the erythropoietin levels. In reactive polycythemia, EPO levels are expected to be low or normal due to an appropriate physiological response to hypoxia.
If EPO levels are elevated, it would raise concerns for primary polycythemia such as polycythemia vera or an EPO-secreting tumor
**Incorrect Option:**

items.text: **Option A:** Philadelphia chromosome is a genetic abnormality associated with chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), a type of blood cancer. However, the given clinical presentation with high hemoglobin, increased total leukocyte count (TLC), and presence of myelocytes and metamyelocytes in the peripheral smear does not suggest CML. Therefore, investigating the Philadelphia chromosome is not indicated in this case.

**Option B:** JAK mutation refers to mutations in the Janus kinase (JAK) genes, which can be seen in certain myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs) such as polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia, and primary myelofibrosis. While the peripheral smear findings of increased myelocytes and metamyelocytes may raise suspicion for an MPN, the high haemoglobin level and low leukocyte count are not consistent with these disorders. Therefore, investigating JAK mutation is not the most appropriate next step.

**Option D:** Bone marrow biopsy with reticulin stain is a more invasive and specific investigation that may be considered if the initial workup, including EPO levels, is inconclusive or if there are additional findings suggestive of a myeloproliferative disorder or myelodysplastic syndrome. However, in the given clinical scenario of a young boy with high haemoglobin, increased TLC with myeloid predominance, and weakness, the more appropriate initial step is to assess EPO levels before proceeding to a bone marrow biopsy. Therefore, the correct option is C, to measure the erythropoietin levels.

blocks.text: Hereditary Spherocytosis (HS)

An inherited disorder caused by intrinsic defects in the red blood cell membrane skeleton, leading to spheroid, less deformable red cells vulnerable to splenic sequestration and destruction. 75% of cases are autosomal dominant. Remaining cases often involve severe forms due to compound heterozygosity (inheritance of two different defects).

**Etiopathogenesis:** HS is marked by a loss of membrane surface area relative to the intracellular volume, leading to spherical red blood cells with reduced or absent central pallor. Spherocytes have decreased deformability, resulting in their retention and destruction in the spleen, causing hemolysis. spectrin, ankyrin, AE1(band 3), protein 4.2 that weakens the vertical connections between the cytoskeletal framework and lipid bilayer.
The ANK1 gene on chromosome 8p produces Ankyrin.
Two proposed mechanisms for membrane loss: In cells with spectrin/ankyrin deficiency. Reduced AE1/protein.
**Clinical features:** 60-70% of patients present with moderate disease, typically in infancy or childhood.
Common findings in children include:

items.text: Anaemia may be asymptomatic
Jaundice is usually intermittent and acholuric (unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia).
>75% show palpable splenomegaly.

blocks.text: Family history.
**Complications:**

items.text: **Gallbladder Disease:** Chronic hemolysis can lead to bilirubinate gallstones.
**Crisis Events:**
**Hemolytic Crisis:** Commonly associated with viral illnesses in childhood; typically mild and self-resolving.

**Aplastic Crisis:** Rare but may cause severe anaemia and require hospitalisation, often linked to parvovirus infection. Typically lasts 10–14 days and may reveal undiagnosed HS in asymptomatic patients.
**Megaloblastic Crisis:** Occurs in patients with increased folate needs, preventable by supplementation.

blocks.text: Other rare complications may include leg ulcers, chronic dermatitis, and skeletal abnormalities.
HS has been associated with increased risks of hematologic malignancies and thrombotic events post-splenectomy.
**Incorrect Options: Iron deficiency anaemia (Option A):** Usually microcytic, hypochromic anaemia with low MCHC, no jaundice, no splenomegaly, and no strong family history.

**Thalassemia minor (Option C):** Presents in infancy with severe anaemia, failure to thrive, hepatosplenomegaly, and bone deformities; MCHC is not elevated, and family history often shows transfusion-dependent anaemia.

**AIHA (Option D):** Can also have spherocytes and jaundice, but is typically acquired, not familial, and the Coombs test is positive. It is often acute/subacute onset, not a chronic familial condition.

The scenario of weakness, fatigue, low haemoglobin, low reticulocyte count, normal WBC and platelet counts, and bone marrow showing a selective reduction in erythroid precursors is consistent with Pure Red Cell Alasia (PRCA), which is characterized by a marked reduction or absence of red blood cell precursors while other hematopoietic cell lines remain normal.
It is a primary marrow disorder in which only erythroid progenitors are suppressed (red cell progenitors are completely absent in severe cases).
**Causes:**

items.text: Associated with neoplasms (thymoma and large granular lymphocytic leukaemia)
Drug exposures
Autoimmune disorders

blocks.text: Iron deficiency anemia is characterized by a deficiency of iron, a key component required for hemoglobin synthesis in red blood cells. Microcytic anemia, where the red blood cells are smaller than normal, is a hallmark of iron deficiency. The patient's symptoms of fatigue, weakness, and pale skin are classic signs of anemia.

Iron deficiency can be caused by inadequate dietary intake, chronic blood loss (such as from menstruation or gastrointestinal bleeding), or poor iron absorption. items.text: **Option A - Alcoholism:** Alcoholism can lead to various health issues, including anemia. However, in this case, the patient's presentation of fatigue, weakness, and pale skin along with microcytic anemia suggests a more specific cause related to iron deficiency.

**Option B - Chronic Kidney Disease:** Chronic kidney disease can cause anemia due to reduced production of erythropoietin (a hormone that stimulates red blood cell production) by the kidneys. However, anemia caused by chronic kidney disease is usually normocytic or normochromic rather than microcytic.

**Option C - Hemolytic Anemia:** Hemolytic anemia results from the destruction of red blood cells at a rate that exceeds their production. blocks.text: IL-6 stands for Interleukin-6, which is a cytokine that plays a crucial role in inflammation and immune responses. In this scenario, the patient presents with microcytic hypochromic anemia, which is often caused by iron deficiency. Ferroportin is a protein that functions as an iron exporter, allowing iron to exit from cells into the bloodstream, where it can be utilized for various physiological processes including red blood cell production.

When ferroportin is inhibited, it leads to reduced iron export from cells and contributes to iron retention within the cells. In chronic inflammatory conditions, such as the one mentioned in the question, there is an increased production of IL-6. IL-6 has been shown to stimulate the production of hepcidin, a peptide hormone synthesized in the liver.

Hepcidin regulates iron homeostasis by binding to ferroportin and causing its internalization and degradation. This action reduces iron export from cells, leading to decreased iron availability for erythropoiesis (red blood cell production).

Consequently, chronic inflammation-induced elevation of IL-6 and subsequent increase in hepcidin levels result in reduced iron absorption and availability for red blood cell formation, leading to microcytic hypochromic anemia.
**Incorrect Options:**

items.text: **Option A - IL-1:** Interleukin-1 is also involved in inflammation and immune responses, but it does not have a direct role in inhibiting ferroportin. It can contribute to inflammation-induced systemic responses.
**Option C - IFN-gamma:** Interferon-gamma (IFN-gamma) is primarily involved in immune responses and has not been directly implicated in the inhibition of ferroportin.

**Option D - TNF-Alpha:** Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha (TNF-alpha) is another cytokine involved in inflammation. It does contribute to the inflammatory response, but it is not the primary cytokine responsible for inhibiting ferroportin.

Multiple myeloma cells produce excess free light chains, either alongside complete immunoglobulins or independently. Due to their small size, free light chains (Bence Jones proteins) can pass through the glomeruli of the kidneys and appear in urine. This is a diagnostic marker for multiple myeloma.

Based on the clinical scenario and the bone marrow findings, the most likely diagnosis is Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML). Blasts in the bone marrow are a pivotal factor in diagnosing different types of leukaemia. When the bone marrow contains over 20% blasts, it indicates acute leukaemia rather than a chronic condition.

Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) is characterised by the rapid proliferation of abnormal myeloid blasts (Myeloblasts are identified by the presence of Auer rods), crowding out normal cells and leading to the symptoms observed.

**Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL) (Option A):** CLL typically presents with mature lymphocytes, not blasts, in the bone marrow, distinguishing it from AML. Histopathology reveals smudge cells. The elevated blast count seen in the bone marrow biopsy is not characteristic of CLL.

**Hodgkin’s Lymphoma (Option C):** HL is diagnosed via lymph node biopsy revealing Reed-Sternberg cells, not through a bone marrow biopsy showing high blast counts. The hallmark of HL is the presence of specific large abnormal lymphocytes, not blasts. HL primarily involves lymph nodes, with systemic symptoms such as night sweats and weight loss.
**Non-Hodgkin’s Lymphoma (NHL) (Option D):** The diagnosis of NHL involves malignant lymphoid cells in affected tissues, not an increased blast percentage in the bone marrow.

blocks.text: Lymphocyte-depleted Hodgkin's lymphoma Histological Features: LDHL is characterised by a scarcity of lymphocytes and many pleomorphic, often bizarre Reed-Sternberg (RS) cells. The cellular environment is typically rich in fibrosis or necrosis. Immunophenotype: The RS cells in LDHL are usually positive for CD15 and CD30 but negative for CD20.

Clinical Presentation: systemic symptoms such as fever, night sweats, and significant weight loss referred to as "B symptoms.” Epidemiology: LDHL is the least common subtype of Hodgkin lymphoma and is more frequently diagnosed in older adults and individuals with HIV infection.

Prognosis: LDHL is associated with a poorer prognosis compared to other Hodgkin lymphoma subtypes due to its more aggressive nature Treatment: Treatment typically involves a combination of chemotherapy and, in some cases, radiation therapy..

Clinical Presentation: Patients often present with painless lymphadenopathy, commonly in peripheral lymph nodes rather than mediastinal involvement. Prognosis: This subtype generally has a favourable prognosis compared to other types of Hodgkin lymphoma due to its lower aggressiveness and higher responsiveness to treatment.

items.text: **Nodular sclerosis Hodgkin lymphoma (Option A):** is the most common subtype, characterised by the presence of lacunar Reed-Sternberg cells and fibrous bands that divide the lymphoid tissue into nodules. These cells are usually positive for CD15 and CD30 but negative for CD20.

**Mixed cellularity Hodgkin lymphoma (Option B):** features a heterogeneous mixture of cells, including Reed-Sternberg cells, lymphocytes, eosinophils, neutrophils, and plasma cells. These cells are typically CD15 and CD30 positive but negative for CD20.

**Lymphocyte-depleted Hodgkin lymphoma (Option D):** is the least common subtype and is characterised by a paucity of lymphocytes and a high number of pleomorphic, often bizarre Reed-Sternberg cells. These cells are usually CD15 and CD30 positive but negative for CD20 and associated with a poorer prognosis

blocks.text: Multiple myeloma is a malignancy of plasma cells, a type of white blood cell that produces antibodies. The clinical presentation of low back ache, progressive pallor (anemia), deranged kidney function tests (KFT), disproportionately increased gamma globulin levels, and lytic lesions on X-ray spine are all consistent with multiple myeloma.
